sections.h2: What speeds up a house sale in Queensbury?
sections.html:
Knowing the tax calendar and the permit history before a buyer asks, then picking a buyer whose closing is free of lender delays. A cash purchase skips appraisal and underwriting, and the deed and town records follow the usual path.

Queensbury is a first-class town in Warren County, set in the southern Adirondack foothills. Its land area of 62.80 square miles is larger than most people expect, and it wraps the city of Glens Falls on three sides. A house here might sit near Lake George, in West Glens Falls or on a rural road, and the school district and fire district on your bills depend on where it is.

sections.h2: What does a seller need to know about the town of Queensbury?
sections.html:
Queensbury is the seat of Warren County government, which operates from a municipal center on U.S. Route 9 south of the village of Lake George. The town was established in 1786 and named for Queen Charlotte, after a colonial land grant, the Queensbury Patent of 1762, drew Quaker settlers in 1763. They left during the Revolutionary War and returned in 1783. Glens Falls incorporated as a city in 1908, and Queensbury has had more residents than that city since the 1980 Census. Its population was 29,169 in 2020, and the Census Bureau's mid-2025 estimate is 29,049, a drop of 0.4% from the 2020 base.

The town's geography shapes what buyers want. Lake George forms the northern edge, the Hudson River runs along the southern boundary, and parts of the western and northern town fall inside the Adirondack Park. Great Escape theme park is in the northwest and West Mountain ski area in the southwest.

  • Hamlets include Glen Lake, West Glens Falls, Kattskill Bay, East Lake George, Oneida Corners and Harrisena.
  • Four school districts cover the town: Queensbury Union Free, Glens Falls City, Hudson Falls Central and Lake George Central.
  • Five fire protection districts operate, named Bay Ridge, North Queensbury, Queensbury Central, South Queensbury and West Glens Falls.
  • SUNY Adirondack and a SUNY Plattsburgh branch campus are in town, and Floyd Bennett Memorial Airport is in the southeast.

The town board has a supervisor plus four council members, one elected from each of four wards, and Queensbury holds five of the 20 seats on the Warren County Board of Supervisors. The town is part of the Glens Falls Metropolitan Statistical Area.

Queensbury has had no police force of its own since 1982. The Warren County Sheriff's Office and the State Police cover the town, which is useful to know when a buyer asks about local services.

sections.h2: How does the Census describe Queensbury homes?
sections.html:
Queensbury leans toward ownership and toward older residents. Owners live in 75.5% of the homes, and 25.9% of residents are 65 or older.

Owners with a mortgage pay a median of $1,943 a month in housing costs, and owners without one pay $689. Workers average a 21.0-minute commute, 92.3% of households have a broadband subscription, and 42.1% of adults aged 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree or higher. Census data shows about $1.4 billion in 2022 retail sales inside the town, so commerce runs well beyond housing. With homes valued around $311,100, a big repair bill takes a visible share of a buyer's offer.

sections.h2: What can Queensbury Buildings and Codes tell an owner before a sale?
sections.html:
The Town of Queensbury's Buildings and Codes office is the place to ask about permits and certificates of occupancy, and the planning and zoning offices handle land use questions.

Ask whether your house has a certificate of occupancy on file for every addition, whether any permits are still open, and whether the town expects any inspection or certificate in connection with the transfer. Put these questions to the office early. A missing certificate for a finished attic or garage conversion is the kind of gap that delays a closing.

A house on septic raises more questions. New York's disclosure form wants the system's age, the date of the last pumping and how often it is pumped, so dig those records out before listing. The same form covers flood zones, wetlands, agricultural districts and fuel tanks, all common on lakeside or rural lots.

sections.h2: How do Queensbury property taxes and assessments work?
sections.html:
Warren County's Real Property Tax Services publishes the yearly calendar Queensbury follows. Around September 1 most school district bills go out, and around January 1 most municipal bills do, each with 30 days free of interest. The county tells new purchasers to contact both the school and municipal tax collectors so billing is not missed.

  • July 1: assessments become final and are used for the coming year's taxes.
  • March 1: Taxable Status Date and the deadline to file any exemption, new or renewal, with the Assessor.
  • April 1: all outstanding taxes become county liens payable to the county Treasurer.
  • May 1: tentative roll filed and change-of-assessment notices mailed.
  • Fourth Tuesday in May: Grievance Day, when the Board of Assessment Review hears assessment complaints.

April 1 is the date that surprises sellers. Once a bill has moved to the county, the payoff must come from the county Treasurer rather than the town tax receiver, so have your attorney order the right figure.

sections.h2: What does the Warren County Clerk charge for a Queensbury deed?
sections.html:
The Warren County Clerk records deeds at the municipal center. The fee schedule lists $40 a document, $5 for the cover sheet, $5 a page, $5 for the TP-584, and $125 for the RP-5217 on qualifying residential or farm property ($250 for other property). Residential deeds also carry a $10 notice of conveyance fee.

The clerk states the state's transfer tax as $4.00 per $1,000, with nothing due at $500 or less. Recording and filing are open from 8:00 a.m. until 3:30 p.m., and electronic recording is available. The clerk's office also records Adirondack Park Agency permits, so look for permit conditions on any parcel inside the Park before closing.

sections.h2: What should a Queensbury owner gather before listing?
sections.html:
A short list saves the most time. Pull the school and town tax bills, find any certificates of occupancy, and note when the septic system or well was last serviced. Near Lake George or inside the Adirondack Park, also check recorded documents for easements or permit conditions a buyer will want to see.

Next, choose a route. A standard listing reaches owner-occupant buyers but relies on inspections and a mortgage approval, while a cash sale closes without a lender. Both end at the county clerk, whose recording window closes at 3:30 p.m., so plan signing times around it.

faqs.q: How do I tell which school district my Queensbury house is in?
faqs.a: The address decides it. Four districts share the town, Queensbury Union Free, Glens Falls City, Hudson Falls Central and Lake George Central, and your school tax bill names yours.

faqs.q: What is the Queensbury tax mailing schedule?
faqs.a: Warren County's calendar has most school bills mailed near September 1 and most municipal bills near January 1, each with 30 interest-free days. Anything unpaid becomes a county lien on April 1.

faqs.q: What does recording a Warren County deed cost?
faqs.a: Budget $40 per document plus $5 for the cover sheet, $5 a page, $5 for the TP-584 and $125 for the RP-5217 on qualifying residential property.

faqs.q: Does a parcel inside the Adirondack Park change the sale?
faqs.a: The Warren County Clerk records Adirondack Park Agency permits, so ask whether any permit is recorded against your parcel and give it to the buyer's attorney.

faqs.q: What is Grievance Day in Queensbury?
faqs.a: It falls on the fourth Tuesday in May, when the Board of Assessment Review hears assessment complaints. Exemption filings are due to the Assessor by March 1.
